instruction: Review each applicable case independently as a complete supplied excerpt. Use your current role and rubric. Assume the mathematics; assess presentation, not new proofs. Do not infer missing introductory prose or import context from another case. A concrete reader obstacle, not a preference for extra prose, is needed for a required repair.

cases.audience: Graduate readers in algorithms and elementary optimization
lines: We seek a certified workload-dependent cost guarantee. The switching budget below is used throughout our cost theorem and determines its parameter regimes. Let the normalized workload x be a positive real number.
Definition. Set q(x)=sqrt(x)+1 for 0<x<=16, and q(x)=x^(1/4)+3 for x>16.
Proposition. The available implementations achieve cost at most q(x).

Proof. Implementation A has certified cost at most sqrt(x)+1, while implementation B has certified cost at most x^(1/4)+3. Choose the implementation with the smaller certified bound. Writing z=x^(1/4), the difference of the bounds is z^2-z-2=(z-2)(z+1), so they agree at x=16 and the displayed branches follow.

lines: The real residual e is the signed difference between an estimate and its target. We measure its magnitude by the usual absolute value.
Thus |e|=e when e>=0 and |e|=-e when e<0. All subsequent error tolerances apply to |e|.

lines: The implementation can choose either of two certified cost bounds u and v, both nonnegative. It always chooses the cheaper guarantee.
Write c=min{u,v}. The following calculations use c as the resulting certified cost bound.

cases.audience: Graduate linear-algebra readers familiar with determinants but not assumed to know graph determinant expansions
lines: We want an expansion of det(I+tBB^T) in which the nonnegative coefficients have a combinatorial meaning. Here B is an oriented incidence matrix of a finite simple graph: an edge column is +1 at one endpoint, -1 at the other, and zero elsewhere. The following algebraic and combinatorial facts will be useful.
Lemma 1. Columns of B indexed by an edge set S are linearly independent exactly when S has no cycle, that is, when S is a forest.

Proof. An oriented cycle gives a signed column dependence. Conversely, remove a leaf of a nonempty forest. Its row forces the coefficient of its unique incident edge to vanish in any dependence; induction finishes the argument.
Lemma 2. For a real r-by-m matrix B, det(I_r+tBB^T)=sum_S t^|S| det(B_S^T B_S), where S ranges over all subsets of columns of size at most r and the empty determinant is one.
Proof. Expand by principal minors and apply the Cauchy-Binet identity to each minor.

We can now read the coefficients as weighted forest counts. The second lemma expands each coefficient into Gram determinants of column sets; the first identifies the nonzero terms as precisely forests. The Gram determinants are nonnegative, making both the coefficient signs and their graph interpretation explicit.

We obtain it by expressing the coefficients as sums of Gram determinants of column sets. Such a determinant is nonzero precisely for independent columns. The next two facts identify these column sets as forests and supply the determinant expansion, linking the coefficients to weighted forest counts.

Proof. An oriented cycle gives a signed column dependence. Conversely, remove a leaf of a nonempty forest. Its row forces the coefficient of its unique incident edge to vanish in any dependence; induction finishes the argument.
Lemma 2. For a real r-by-m matrix B, det(I_r+tBB^T)=sum_S t^|S| det(B_S^T B_S), where S ranges over all subsets of columns of size at most r and the empty determinant is one.
Proof. Expand by principal minors and apply the Cauchy-Binet identity to each minor.
Together these facts give the announced weighted-forest expansion, with nonnegative Gram-determinant weights.
